chapter_theme: Swamimalai (சுவாமி மலை, 2 of 3): courtesans and the arts of 'Kama's scripture', the diseased and ageing body, poems wasted on patrons, a lovesick girl's song, and pleas for the release the Agamas teach, for servanthood among devotees, and, uniquely, for Murugan to be born as the poet's own child; the praise returns again and again to Murugan teaching his father Siva.
structure_note: Courtesan and desire songs (219, 224 to 227, 230); the body and age (217, 229); patronage (220); an akam song (221); Death (228); devotion and doctrine (222, 223, 231); and 218, which brings the Lord into household life.

217.reading: The poet catalogues the body, nerves, bones, flesh, fat, phlegm, the cave of blood, semen, worms, filth and hair, and its diseases, leprosy, abscess, swelling, colic and bile, and asks whether he must fade in the world, taking up again and again this hut of five elements with all its thoughts, cravings, pride and deceits, birth after birth. The praise is a battle in drum syllables at the Krauncha hill, and tells how Murugan seized the lotus-born by his tuft and rapped his head; he is the merchant who came to Valli's millet field and the guru of Siva whom the freed souls praise.
217.nuance: The fullest anatomy of disgust so far in the book. கமலத்தனை மணிக்குடுமி பற்றி ... பல குட்டி: Brahma punished by Murugan, though Om is not named here; செட்டி வடிவு: Murugan disguised as a merchant to woo Valli. Some disease names and two garbled words (சங்முளை, வங்க்முடே) are uncertain.

218.reading: The poet asks Murugan to come into the household life that the world's maya has given him, as the child his wife carries ten months and brings forth, so that he may play with him on his head, at his eyes and face and on his shoulders, take him on his lap, and receive kisses from his jewelled mouth every day. The praise names the one who came to embrace the hunter girl, the guru who told the one great meaning within the ancient Veda, Murugan of Erakam who let the poet see his feet, and the lord with the battle-vel on the Kaveri's north bank.
218.nuance: மணிவாயின் முத்தி: முத்தி is the child's kiss (முத்தம்) and also mukti, so the plea asks for both at once. The Lord is asked into household life, as the poet's son, rather than as an escape from it.

219.reading: The poet describes women with eyes like fish and spears, who say they have no wish for money and cling like a wife, then seize a man's legs and hair and quarrel, and asks whether he, the Lord's servant, should be thrown into turmoil in this snare of deceitful lust. The praise pictures the Kaveri carrying cardamom, cloves and areca around Erakam, the vel that Indra, holder of the thunderbolt, worships, and the lord who split Krauncha, the sea and Sura.
219.nuance: பணத்தில் ஆசை இலை என்ற: the protest that she does not want money belongs to the trick. The second and third lines are hard to divide, so the picture of the women is tentative.

220.reading: The poet describes singing for patrons: thinking 'these men will give', he made bee-messages, envoy poems, garlands of verse, sindhu and kalitturai for love of wealth, praising their hands and heads, only to be told 'come another time' and tossed a coin with contempt by fools; he asks that this wandering end and that he be given the love that rules him with joy here and hereafter under Murugan's two feet. The praise pictures Gurumalai's waters, where storks, herons and anril birds startle at leaping vaalai fish as if the sea had roared in.
220.nuance: A poet's complaint about patronage that names the genres he wasted on men (வண்டு விடு தூது, கவிமாலை, சிந்து, கலித்துறை). The remedy is not to give up song but to turn it to the Lord. A few lines (வருமதுவொ போதும்) are hard to divide.

221.reading: In the voice of someone close to a girl in love, the song asks whether she, her breasts thrilling, should be left wavering and worn in mind by the taunts of the women who gather in the street, by the moon rising red over the sea like the sun, and by the arrows of Kama. The praise names the vel that split a hill in two, Murugan who stands at Tiruverakam, the poet who tells the Vedas and Tamil works in order, and the lord who frees the fettered feet of Vishnu, Brahma and the gods.
221.nuance: Akam conventions throughout: the street's gossip, the evening moon that burns like the sun, Kama's bow. The speaker is not named; it reads as a mother or friend, as in 24. அருமறை தமிழ்நூல் அடைவே தெரிந்துரைக்கும் புலவோனே: Murugan as poet of Veda and Tamil alike.

222.reading: The poet asks that he not stumble, worn out, mingling at the doors of the wicked, nor lose his knowledge and sink deep, but, speaking the words of those who praise Murugan, live in joy and stand worshipping the two fragrant lotus feet. The praise names the guru whom Siva praised for telling the word, the bridegroom moved by Devayanai whom Indra gave, and the lord in yoga on Gurumalai, worshipped by Kesava.
222.nuance: நாசர் தம் கடை அதனில் விரவி: the doors of the wicked may be those of patrons, as in 220, or the company of bad men generally. The guru 'for the word' (வாசகம் புகல) is the Swamimalai teaching of Siva.

223.reading: The poet asks for the jnana-release that runs through the twenty-eight Agamas and their four ways, as he has spoken it daily in songs on the Lord's feet, so that, with neither the Lord saying 'you are other' nor he saying 'I am other', he may live in union, and that Murugan tell him 'see' the Supreme above the six supports. The praise names the guru who taught Siva and his circle the understanding of jnana, the bridegroom of the hunter girl, Murugan of Swamimalai by the Kaveri, and the son of Kali, Bala, Shakti, the left half of Kama's foe.
223.nuance: நாலாறு நாலு: twenty-eight, the number of the Saiva Agamas; the 'four' may be the four paths. நீ வேறு எனாதிருக்க நான் வேறு எனாதிருக்க: non-difference asked from both sides. ஷடாதாரத்தின் மீதே பராபரம்: the Supreme above the six centres of yoga. The counting is the likeliest reading, not a certain one.

224.reading: The poet describes women who sit in moonlight choosing flowers for their hair, whose spear-eyes reach their ear-rings, whose words drive out thought, and who practise without measure the arts of Kama's treatise, and calls himself the deceiver deluded in lovemaking with them; he asks for grace to rule him. The praise names Uma, who stood as the single source of the seven worlds, the gods' worlds, Kailasa, Meru, life and the five elements, as the one by whose grace Kumara grew, and the vel against Sura, at Gurumalai rising like a peak.
224.nuance: மதன் நூல் (garbled in the source): Kama's treatise as the women's discipline, as மதனாகமம் in 230. கபடன், deceiver, is the poet's name for himself. The praise gives Uma the place of first cause.

225.reading: A short song: the poet asks whether the love of women whose faces shine like the full moon and whose eyes are arrows can be a true bond, and asks for Murugan's holy feet now. The praise names Vishnu's nephew, death to the demon clans, Valli's bridegroom, at Gurumalai.
225.nuance: உனதிரு வடிவியினி is garbled; it most likely reads உன திருவடி இனி, 'your holy feet now', though திருவடிவு, 'holy form', is possible.

226.reading: The poet asks whether he must wander as great infatuation rises for women whose breasts carry ornaments, whose eyes are swords, whose hair is full of flowers and whose smile is like moonlight. The praise centres on Uma, the light on the left side of Siva who wears the serpent, named Dakini, Tripurai and Narani, and names Murugan Saravana the teacher, Guha the treasure of compassion, at Gurumalai.
226.nuance: மாமயல் நிலையெழவே அலைவது: infatuation as a state that rises and drives him wandering. As in 32, the praise dwells on the Mother more than on Murugan.

227.reading: The poet asks whether the false lovemaking of women who sell themselves can be sweet: they promise many loves for one hour's gain, praise many men, talk away shame, give poison and snatch great wealth. The praise names Rama, whose arrow felled the demon who lifted the mountain, as uncle, Murugan who hears with delight the Tamil of those who know the kavyas, and the lord at Tiruverakam who gave Siva the teaching due to him.
227.nuance: விலைமாதர் பொய்க்கலவி: the courtesan's love called false, in the Kural's own terms. விடமே கொடுத்து may be a love-drug or poison. சிவனார் தமக்குரிய உபதேச வித்தை: the teaching to Siva, the Swamimalai myth.

228.reading: The poet asks that Death not come near him but that he worship at Murugan's holy feet. The praise names the son given by Siva of the crescent, river and flowers, the bridegroom who pressed the hunter girl's feet, the nephew of Vishnu who showed grace to the crow that lost one eye, the young one who freed the gods from prison and comes on the peacock, at Swamimalai, whose vel dried the sea.
228.nuance: காதும் ஒருவிழி காகம் உற அருள் மாயன்: the crow that lost one eye to Rama's arrow and was spared, an act of grace. Murugan pressing Valli's feet (பாதம் வருடிய) matches 209.

229.reading: The poet describes women whose eyes are arrows hidden in the bow of the bodiless Kama, and asks whether one day, before they scorn him as his scented hair whitens and youth slips away, Murugan will cut the root of the births he has taken without pause and give his sweet feet. The praise names the peacock that shakes the seven worlds and eight mountains, the young one who gave the gods back their life, Murugan of Swamimalai, and the lord who taught the jnana his father asked to learn.
229.nuance: The argument against desire is the women's scorn when he ages, not their deceit (compare 34). தாதை கற்க வினவ ஓதுவித்த: the father asks and the son teaches.

230.reading: The poet confesses that he was deluded by women with fragrant hair through the arts of Kama's scripture, drank their lips and was bound to their breasts, and asks Murugan, not forgetting his favour to this lonely one, to bear with his faults and grant the great life that holds to his feet. The praise names Guha who gave the teaching to Siva as guru, the bridegroom of the hunter girl, the young one of the Kaveri from the western hills, and Vishnu's nephew who cut off the demons' heads.
230.nuance: மதனாகமம்: Kama's Agama, a pointed phrase in a Saiva poet, as if love had its own scripture. பிழையே பொறுத்து: the plea is for forgiveness, not reward.

231.reading: The poet asks that, forgetting the love that drowned him in women's breasts, with the light of supreme jnana growing and longing for the six faces without tiring, he strew arugu, thali, kuvalai and karandai flowers on the feet, and be given the one way of servanthood that grows from love among devotees who melt beside themselves. The praise names the vel that dried the sea, the peacock hero who drank Uma's milk and circled the seven worlds, Valli's bridegroom, at Swamimalai of groves.
231.nuance: அவசமாகி உருகு தொண்டருடன் அதாகி: the poet asks to become one with the melting devotees; அடிமையாகு முறைமை is devotional service here, the opposite of the bondage to women in 213.

links.note: The Naladiyar gives one picture, a pot of filth leaking from nine openings under a dark skin; 217 takes the body apart organ by organ and disease by disease, and adds the hut of five elements taken up birth after birth.
The Kural finds the body's joy in touching one's children; 218 asks for that very joy with the Lord as the child on the lap, and puns the child's kiss (முத்தி) into release.
Both are songs of a girl lovesick for Murugan, voiced by someone near her, with the evening moon and Kama's arrows; 221 adds the street's gossip.
Tirumular counts the Agamas twenty-eight, heard from Siva; 223 asks for the release that runs through the same twenty-eight, so the plea rests on the Siddhanta canon.
Both call the courtesan's embrace false (பொய்ம்மை முயக்கம், பொய்க்கலவி) because it is for wealth; the Kural likens it to a corpse in a dark room, 227 adds poison and wealth snatched.

Tirumular lists the body's constituents, இரதம் உதிரம் இறைச்சி தோல் மேதை ... அத்தி ... மச்சை ... சுக்கிலம், and calls them பாழாம் உபாதி, a perishing adjunct. 217 runs the same inventory, நரம்பு, எலும்பு, தசை, இரத்தம், சுக்கிலம், to call the body a குடில் of five elements taken up birth after birth. The same catalogue serves Tirumular's analysis of tattvas and the song's disgust at rebirth.

Tirumular's women cling like grass in a storm (புயலுறும் புல்லின் புணர்ந்தவரேயினும்) and say 'stay near' (சார இரும் என்பார்), then talk with others and are gone. 219's women say they have no wish for money (பணத்தில் ஆசையிலை), lie close like a wife for all time, then seize legs and hair in a quarrel. Both make the profession of attachment itself the trap.

The Naladiyar's man of worth, even when fortune leaves him, will not stand with bowed neck behind fools who hoard wealth (அருத்தம் செறிக்கும் அறிவிலார் பின்சென்று எருத்திறைஞ்சி). 220 confesses doing exactly that: making envoy poems and verse garlands for patrons, walking to fools (மடையரிடமே நடந்து) and being tossed a coin with 'come another time'. The song turns the Naladiyar's rule into a poet's confession and a plea to sing for the Lord instead.

The Kural says no help exceeds good company and nothing brings more affliction than bad (நல்லினத்தி னூங்குந் துணையில்லை தீயினத்தின் அல்லற் படுப்பதூஉம் இல்). 222 asks not to be worn out mingling at the doors of the wicked (நாசர் தம் கடையதனில் விரவி) and sinking, but to speak the words of those who praise Murugan. The song applies the Kural's choice of company to devotion.

Tirumular says that on nearing him there is no difference such as 'I' and 'you' (நானென நீயென வேறில்லை), like flesh and its life. 223 asks for union in which neither the Lord says 'you are other' nor the poet 'I am other' (நீவேறெனாதிருக்க நான்வேறெனாதிருக்க). The song asks for, as the fruit of the Agamas' jnana, the non-difference Tirumular states.

858 ends its long account of a miser's life by asking for the supreme bliss where 'you and I' become one enjoyment (ஏக போகமாய் நீயு நானுமாய்). 223 asks for the same goal in doctrinal terms, non-difference from both sides after the Agamas' four ways. Read together they show the book's goal of release is union, not only reaching the feet.

Tirumular's first mother (ஆதி முதல்வி) stands with her power as the Veda, the moving and unmoving, the five elements (ஐம்பூதம்) and the many lives. 224's praise names Uma as the single source (ஒருமுதலாகி நின்ற உமை) of the seven worlds, the gods' worlds, Kailasa, the golden mountain, lives and the five elements. The praise half of a courtesan song carries Tirumular's doctrine of Shakti as first cause.

Tirumular names the Shakti of the Tripura chakra திரிபுரை, சுந்தரி, ... நாரணி, Manonmani, and says she stands as many. 226's praise names Murugan's mother டாகினி திரிபுரை நாரணி, the light on Siva's left side. The song draws its names of Uma from the same list of the Goddess that Tirumular gives as the forms of one power.

Tirumular tells his hearers to praise the lord of Kailasa and stand telling the nature of the one who kicked Death (கூற்றுதைத்தான் தன்மை கூறிநின்று உய்ம்மினே). 228 asks that Death not come near him (காலன் எனை அணுகாமல்) but that he worship at Murugan's holy feet (திருகாலில் வழிபட). The song makes the son's feet the refuge from Death that Tirumular finds in the father's.

Tirumular says the women who once desired him like sugarcane juice now find him bitter as the kaanjiram fruit (கரும்பொத்துக் காஞ்சிரங் காயுமொத்தேனே). 229 asks for the feet before the women scorn him (இகழ) as his hair whitens and youth hides away. Both argue against desire from the women's own turning away in old age, not from their deceit.

Tirumular says the Lord, like a parent who sees both the ways and the faults of the sons he begot, does without anger what fits each soul (பெற்ற புதல்வர்போல் ... குற்றமுங் கண்டு ... செற்றமிலாச் செய்கை). 230 asks Murugan to bear with his faults (பிழையே பொறுத்து) after a life deluded by Kama's Agama. Tirumular's teaching is the ground for the song's plea for forgiveness rather than reward.

On the reading that அவன் is the devotee, Tirumular says those who draw near him and love him can draw near Siva too (அவன்பால் அணுகியே அன்புசெய் வார்கள் சிவன்பால் அணுகுதல் செய்யவும் வல்லன்). 231 asks to become one with the devotees who melt beside themselves (உருகு தொண்டருடன் அதாகி) and to be given servanthood that grows from love. Both make the company of devotees the way to the Lord.

source_issues: Song 218: corrupt character in உடலு஡றி (line 2, probably உடலூறி).
Song 224: corrupt character in மதனு஡லின் (line 4, probably மதனூலின், 'Kama's treatise').
Song 229: corrupt character in சிலையி னு஡டோ ளித்த (line 3, probably சிலையினூடு ஒளித்த).
Song 217: unflagged garbles சங்முளை (line 3) and வங்க்முடே (line 6), apparently the same dropped ஊ (மூளை, அங்கமூடே).
